verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents, of David. If not [for] YHWH who was for us — let Israel say, please —
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the road up to Zion, David's song. If the LORD had not been ours, if he had not stood with us in the hour of need — let Israel say it now, let the whole people say it aloud —
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse opens on a hanging 'if': the sentence is a cliff edge, and the speaker leaves it open so the whole crowd can step off it together. The line is a liturgy, not a private memory. 'Let Israel say' is a cue to the pilgrims on the road up to Jerusalem, and the first half of the verse waits for them to answer. Play it as a call, with the people's response coming in verse 2.

The small phrase 'who was for us' (שֶׁהָיָה לָנוּ) is the pivot. English 'on our side' is a fair rendering of the preposition: Ibn Ezra reads לנו like the soldier's question in Joshua 5:13, 'Are you for us (הֲלָנוּ) or for our adversaries?', and Radak glosses לנו as 'with us'. The KJV's 'on our side' therefore keeps the sense, though its 'it had not been the Lord who' is smoother than the Hebrew, which has no 'it'. The KJV also keeps the Hebrew order of the clauses, so it reads 'If it had not been the Lord who was on our side, now may Israel say'. Metzudat David notes that the sentence is really to be read with the clauses reversed (סרס המקרא): 'Let Israel say now: if not for the LORD who was with us...'. That is how most modern speakers will hear it, and the dramatic layer follows it.

'A song of the ascents' (שִׁיר הַמַּעֲלוֹת) marks the pilgrim collection, Psalms 120–134. The Targum takes 'ascents' as the steps of the deep (מַסוּקִין דִתְהוֹמָא), and Meiri and Radak hear exile in the psalm. The title 'of David' (לְדָוִד) is a Hebrew preposition that can mean by, for or belonging to David, so the director should not stage David himself as the singer.

philological_notes.note: 'The ascents': the label of Psalms 120–134. It is most often read as songs for the pilgrimage up to Jerusalem; the KJV's 'degrees' means 'steps', and the Targum reads steps of the deep. The meaning is uncertain.

'Who was for us'. The relative שֶׁ is the late, colloquial particle in place of אֲשֶׁר. Ibn Ezra compares לנו to Joshua 5:13 (הֲלָנוּ אַתָּה אִם לְצָרֵינוּ) and Radak glosses it 'with us'; the sense is partisan loyalty, 'for' as opposed to 'against'.

A jussive with the particle נָא: 'let it say, please'. Ibn Ezra glosses נא as 'now', as in other places in Scripture, and Metzudat David moves the clause to the front. The call invites the congregation to answer.

verses.translation_literal: If not YHWH, who was for us, when rose up against us man.
verses.translation_dramatic: Had the LORD not been for us, in the hour men rose up against us.
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain returns word for word, and the second time it gets the plot: 'when man rose up against us'. The condition is now set. A singer who drops the first clause here would lose the effect, because the repetition is the beat of the song, a beat the crowd can join before it knows the words.

The Hebrew has the singular אָדָם, 'man' or 'Adam', with no article. Ibn Ezra reads it as a collective, 'men', and the KJV and ASV supply that. The singular gives a different feel: the enemy is not named by nation or by army but by the plainest word for a human being. They are only people, and that makes the LORD's presence the sharper contrast. Radak places this in the exile. The verb קוּם, 'rise up against', is the language of an uprising or a levy, and the actors should stand up on it.

philological_notes.note: Singular 'man', read as a collective by Ibn Ezra. The enemy is left unnamed and merely human.

verses.translation_literal: Then alive they would have swallowed us, in the burning of their nose against us.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then they would have swallowed us down, living, still breathing, while their anger burned hot against us.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the enemy becomes an animal, or a mouth. The verb בָּלַע is 'swallow' and is the same verb used for the earth that swallowed Korah (Numbers 16:30-32), where the victims also go down alive. The word חַיִּים, 'alive', is placed before the verb to stress it: not killed first, then eaten, but eaten whole. Radak and Metzudat David explain the image: a hungry creature normally cooks its meat, but these enemies were so greedy that they would not wait.

The literal expression for anger is 'in the burning of their nose'. אַף is the nose and also anger, because anger flares the nostrils, and the verb חָרָה is 'to burn'. The KJV 'when their wrath was kindled' is a fair idiom but loses the body. Rashi says בַּחֲרוֹת is an infinitive like בַּעֲשׂוֹת in Ezekiel 23:21. The KJV 'quick' is archaic for 'alive' and no longer reads as such; the modern ear hears speed.

philological_notes.note: 'Their nose', meaning 'their anger'. The root imagery is the flaring or burning nostril.
'Then'. The final yod is extra, as Radak and Meiri note, and it is a poetic form of אָז. It opens vv. 3, 4 and 5 and drives the sequence.

verses.translation_literal: Then the waters would have overflowed us, a torrent would have passed over our soul;
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the waters would have closed over us, flooding the dry bed in a roar; a torrent would have gone over our very souls.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture changes from teeth to water. Verse 3 had the enemy as a beast; here he is a flash flood. In Judah the wadis (נַחַל) are dry for most of the year and then, after a storm in the hills, a wall of water comes down in minutes. Everyone in the audience has seen a gully fill, or knows someone caught in one. Say the line as the sound of that water arriving.

'Overflowed' (שָׁטַף) is the verb of floods. The KJV's 'overwhelmed' is a little vague for it; the Hebrew has the sweep of a surge, not a weight. The KJV also turns the singular 'torrent' into 'the stream', and 'had gone over' fits the Hebrew perfect, but a 'would have' is truer to the conditional: all of it is what did not happen. Notice the tense chain. Hebrew uses past forms for the unreal, and the whole verse sits under the 'if not' of verse 1.

The odd form נַחְלָה carries a final ה, and the accent falls on the first syllable (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri). It is not a locative 'towards', as the STEPBible tag suggests, and Rashi's different reading (a word for 'sickness') is not the one the commentators generally follow. Treat it as a paragogic ה on 'torrent'. The torrent passes 'over our soul' (נַפְשֵׁנוּ): נֶפֶשׁ is the throat, the breath and the life, so the picture is of water closing over the neck and mouth. Meiri also notes that the line can mean the body, or that in the body's distress the soul grows weary. The next verse repeats the phrase.

philological_notes.note: 'A torrent'. The final ה is not a direction marker here: Radak and Meiri say it is an added ה, and that the accent is on the first syllable (מלעיל). Rashi reads it as 'sickness' (חולי); that reading is not followed here. The wadi is the Hebrew picture of a flash flood.
'They had overflowed us': the verb of a flood sweeping over and through. Metzudat David reads the waters as the mass of enemies, and Radak reads them as an image for troubles.

'Our soul', with the throat or neck of the body as its older sense; the water passes over the person, as if over the neck. Meiri takes it as the body, or as the soul wearied in bodily distress; Malbim contrasts it with the body (גוף).

verses.translation_literal: Then it would have passed over our soul, the waters, the seething.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then over us, over our lives, would have gone the waters, the seething waters.
verses.directors_commentary:
The line is a refrain with a twist: 'passed over our soul' is repeated from verse 4, and the subject is saved until the end, 'the waters, the seething'. Radak and Metzudat David both observe that Hebrew poetry repeats a point two and three times for strength. This is the third 'then' in a row, and it is the loudest. Build the three verses as one rising swell: jaws, flood, and the flood again with a name.

הַזֵּידוֹנִים is a hapax legomenon, a word found nowhere else in the Bible. It comes from the root meaning to boil or seethe, near זָדוֹן, 'arrogance', so that the waters are both foaming and insolent, water that does not know its limit. The KJV 'proud' catches the second sense only. Radak says they flow 'in wickedness and arrogance', and Meiri notes another reading, 'the waters of the arrogant', that is, arrogant people. Because עָבַר is singular, Ibn Ezra reads it as continuing the 'torrent' of verse 4.

philological_notes.note: A hapax legomenon, 'the seething', 'the raging'. It is related to the root זיד, 'to boil up', and to זָדוֹן, 'arrogance', so it joins both foaming and pride. Meiri records a reading 'the waters of the arrogant'.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed be YHWH, who did not give us prey to their teeth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed be the LORD, who did not hand us over, torn and bleeding, to their teeth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The grammar breaks at once. All the 'ifs' and 'thens' of verses 1-5 stop, and the singers shout a blessing. This is the release the audience has been waiting for. The tone should change from a held breath to an outburst.

The picture of the mouth from verse 3 comes back here, in the plain image of teeth. טֶרֶף is 'prey', the torn flesh of an animal's kill: the word is used for the lion's food (Genesis 49:9; Amos 3:4). The KJV 'prey to their teeth' is accurate, but the BBE's 'wounded by their teeth' is weaker. The verb 'give' is the verb for handing over a captive, so the LORD is the one who could have surrendered them and did not. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David connect this verse to the swallowing of verse 3. Note also that the Hebrew's 'prey' is not the animal but the meat, and the people were the meat.

philological_notes.note: 'Prey', torn flesh, the kill of a predator. It is used for what a lion carries to its den (Nahum 2:13). The verb 'give' makes it a handing-over.

verses.translation_literal: Our soul, like a bird, has escaped from the snare of fowlers; the snare is broken, and we, we have escaped.
verses.translation_dramatic: Our life, like a small bird, has slipped away from the fowlers' trap. The snare lies broken, and we, we are out, we are free.
verses.directors_commentary:
A third image arrives, and it is the gentlest: a bird. After the jaws and the flood, the singers say that the people were a bird in a net, and the net broke. The picture comes from ordinary Israelite life, where small birds were caught with a spring snare or a net on the ground. The word פַּח is that snare, which Amos 3:5 shows closing on a bird. Radak and Meiri make the logical point that a bird caught in a snare cannot get out unless the snare itself is broken, so the escape is not the bird's own doing. That is the whole theology of the psalm in one picture.

The verb נִמְלְטָה, 'escaped', is a niphal and is repeated at the end as נִמְלָטְנוּ. The first uses 'our soul' with a feminine verb, the second uses 'we' with the first plural, so the line moves from the life to the people. The KJV 'is escaped' is an old perfect, now odd to hear, and 'the fowlers' is correct but the KJV obscures the abrupt sudden stop. The final 'and we' (וַאֲנַחְנוּ) is an emphatic pronoun with a long form, so actors should lean on it: we, ourselves. Metzudat David adds that the breaking of the snare means the wicked fall.

philological_notes.note: 'Escaped', a niphal. The root recurs in 'we have escaped' at the end of the verse, framing the line with the same verb, first for 'soul' (feminine singular) and then for 'we'.
A bird snare or trap. The line says the snare 'was broken', which Radak and Meiri take to mean that a bird cannot be freed unless the snare is destroyed.
'Fowlers', those who lay snares. The form is a participle of a root that occurs mainly in this verse and in Hosea 9:8 and Jeremiah 5:26.

verses.translation_literal: Our help is in the name of YHWH, maker of heaven and earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Our help is in the name of the LORD, the maker of heaven and earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends in plain speech, and the actors should drop the volume. After the heavy imagery, the closing line is a statement of fact, said slowly, almost as a creed. The Hebrew for 'help' is עֵזֶר, the word of Genesis 2:18, the help that is needed because one cannot stand alone.

'In the name of YHWH' means help that comes through the invoked name, not through the people's own strength. Metzudat David says so directly: the help comes by mention of the name, not by the power of our hands. The tag 'maker of heaven and earth' closes the argument. The enemies of verses 2-5 are pictured as men, beasts, floods and fowlers, and the LORD is the maker of all of those: the sea, the wadi and the sky the birds fly in. Meiri and Malbim read it as a claim that the LORD can change the natural order. In a world where each nation's god belonged to a patch of land or a river, this is a claim over every domain. The KJV has 'who made', which is accurate, but 'עֹשֵׂה' is a participle, 'maker', a title and not a past event.

philological_notes.note: 'Our help'. The noun is the one used in Genesis 2:18 for the 'help' that is needed. Here it is not the people's own strength but help from outside them.
A participle used as a title, 'maker of heaven and earth', which makes the LORD's power cover both the upper and lower worlds, as Ibn Ezra and Radak say.
